To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the most stringent mitigation targets are technically feasible but become more costly the later action is delayed.
mitigation to stringent targets is feasible, but requires a combination of strong policy action, a rapid transition to low-carbon technologies, and strong progress on energy efficiency.

Mitigation costs are higher if mitigation action is delayed, if there is limited deployment of key technologies (nuclear, CCS, wind, solar) or energy efficiency, if there is a high discount rate, and if carbon capture and storage is not deployed in the power sector.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether the world can meet the 2 deg target.
the following question: How do the latest model-based mitigation studies inform our knowledge on the costs, technologies, and other impacts of limiting global warming to 1.5 or 2 degC?

the question of how to get the best value for money out of climate policy and the results suggest that the best value for the climate is to act now, to act fast, to act smart and to act with the world.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, according to models, mitigation to the 2 deg target is feasible but costly and challenging, but the extent of the costs and challenges depend on the model assumptions.
mitigation towards 2 degC requires a major transformation of energy systems, and is technically and economically feasible, but the costs are high and the time window is short.
mitigation is feasible, but only at a very high cost if delayed, and only with the deployment of a broad range of technologies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the latest generation of models and studies show that mitigation to stringent levels of global warming is feasible but costly, particularly in the case of delayed action.
the 2 deg C target remains feasible, but the costs of meeting it will rise if we delay action.
the costs of mitigation to 2 degrees are high but manageable and that the costs of inaction are much higher.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is no single, unique, optimal pathway to 2 deg C.
the costs of 2 degC mitigation are highly sensitive to assumptions on key input parameters and that there is considerable scope for further work to improve the quality of the evidence base.
the 2 deg target remains feasible, but the window of opportunity is narrowing.
